#1126. As I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, the raw emotion and magic of Old Trafford was all around me. It was a stark reminder that the fans and the place they flock to really are Man United's greatest gift, writes IAN HERBERT

Published: 07:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 06:22 EDT, 5 November 2026

The sound came rolling down in waves, crashing down around us as I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, in the moments after Manchester United had conceded a most dreadful first goal. It was low and sonorous and quite extraordinary, really.

When a club go nine games without winning and fall behind again, you expect an air of sullen resignation – not that ‘UNITED’ which took hold and grew in a collective, magical act of defiance.

Much more would follow in a significant escalation of protest against the Glazers and their minority partner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. But in that moment – and once more when Roma’s second goal threatened to turn this into a catastrophe – it was just about the terraces and their team. A fanbase refusing to go gently into a night of quiet desperation.

Much has been made of the supposed need to let go of a history which has weighed heavy on this club since Sir Alex stepped away. In turn, United try to release it and then cleave to it again, blindly staggering around in their wilderness.

But on Tuesday night, in the stand bearing the great manager’s name, you looked around and were reminded of how the folk memory of Law, Best, Charlton, Cantona and Rooney is such a powerful weapon. It binds the fans back to what was once great. It is fuel.

What those fans brought into the stadium was not a naive and nostalgic sentimentality. They still demanded the best of the players. There is a clear acceptance among many that Bruno Fernandes is trying to repair things, but when he went down theatrically and protested about a challenge, he was told, ‘stop whinging’.

Michael Carrick celebrates Manchester United's victory over Roma on an incredible Old Trafford Champions League night

Matheus Cunha reacts after scoring United's third goal in their comeback win

This is a discerning, intelligent football public. ‘Standards’ is the word on that banner that’s been flying on the Stretford End.

But the collective view before kick-off was that if the players gave fully, then the fans were with them. ‘I just need to know they’re trying,’ said my friend Jocelyn, as we threaded our way through the crowds to the stadium.

Harry Maguire, who has lived this period of United struggle in the raw and was terribly exposed in a wretched first half, still wore that perpetual look of defiance on his face. When United were fatefully awarded the retaken penalty kick, some were saying that Maguire should be handed the ball. ‘At least he’ll put his foot through it.’

There was a frustration with the way that moments of promise broke down, as passes from Kobbie Mainoo and Carlos Baleba went astray. And with the time it takes Senne Lammens to decide how to distribute the ball, which slows United dreadfully. Yet a recognition of the fight shown by individuals who were patently playing for and engaging with the struggles of Carrick, while contending with a scorching scrutiny.

The shadow on the wall was the owners, of course. It was significant that the chants of derision for them struck up on the Stretford End each time United scored. As if to say that the green and gold campaign won’t fade with the slightest prospect of hope this time. There were tennis balls, balloons and a sense that something is building.

Even now, after 21 years, do the Glazers, hiding in their Florida redoubt, really know that they are playing with fire? This now feels as visceral as Liverpool fans’ hate for Tom Hicks and George Gillett Jnr, 20 years ago.

That club’s fans found ways of getting them out. They email-bombed every outfit that seemed ready to offer to help them, from Royal Bank of Scotland to US equity firm Blackstone. The audible boos when the tennis balls rained down after 20 minutes and five seconds – 20.05 represents the year the Glazers staged their leveraged buy-out – suggests protests affecting play are unwelcome for some and perhaps many. Yet the fury is unbridled. The centre may not hold this time.

The night, however, was about the power of this place to do extraordinary things. Even when Bryan Mbeumo crashed a golden chance to equalise against the post in the early stages of the comeback, you sensed something was afoot.

You’re so close to the pitch in the lower tiers of the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand that you feel you can almost reach out and touch the players. As the stadium gave, so they received. Fernandes marshalled. Youri Tielemans made a difference. Matheus Cunha seized the game by the throat.

Cunha and Shea Lacey race towards the jubilant crowd after United's third goal

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again. At the end Diego Dalot was flat out on his back before us. Mason Mount, who’d been on the field barely five minutes, was in delirium and the post-match acknowledgement of fans by Carrick with his players felt like a victory lap. It meant that much.

The Carrick anthem was still being sung on the concourses as we flooded out under the clear night sky, and you knew for sure in that moment why no one wants the distinctly average names like Eddie Howe, Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann being touted for this job.

‘I don’t want us to start all over again,’ Jocelyn told me, still trying to compute what we’d just seen, after we'd joined the departing throng. ‘I want Carrick to do it. I want more nights like this.’

We learned in the aftermath that Carrick’s career-saving half-time speech had involved him telling his players how Old Trafford could do this. ‘I don't like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do and the history and what's gone before too much, but it's there,’ he said. ‘This place does magical things. It's done it before and it'll do it over and over again.’

Yes, that really did encapsulate the essence of a night on which we discovered, once more, that the fans and the place they flock to really are Manchester United's greatest gift.

#1123. Why Tottenham's 'rock' Jan Paul van Hecke is being compared to Bobby Moore and Stuart Pearce: 'Releasing the beast', a 'Zeeland Army' watching his every move and how high-risk passing is paying off

Published: 07:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 07:14 EDT, 5 November 2026

With his roots in a humble fishing community, World Cup pedigree in the family and glowing comparisons to a couple of England legends, it is perhaps no surprise to find Jan Paul van Hecke emerging as Tottenham's anchorman after a turbulent start to the season.

Van Hecke's strength of character shone through when things went badly awry and Spurs sank to the bottom of the Premier League, winless in the first five games, then rose from the depths with 10 points from the next four.

His ability and influence would never have been in doubt as far as Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi was concerned, having worked with Van Hecke for two years at Brighton. The 26-year-old Dutch centre-half leaves a positive impression wherever he plays.

'JP is a real force,' says Peter Maas, technical director of NAC Breda, where Van Hecke began his professional career. 'He is a rock. He will never back off. He will never let his team down. Never, never. He is truly one of a kind. A good lad with a good heart.

'I've always compared his presence and commitment to Stuart Pearce, "Psycho" back in the '80s and '90s. He was crazy, eh? Every now and then, JP will release the beast and let everything out.

'But he can play football, too. He can defend in an old-school way, but he can also build play in the modern way and is certainly more composed now.'

Jan Paul van Hecke has been Tottenham's anchorman this season, as they recovered from a woeful start to take 10 points from their last four league games

He tops Spurs' charts for clearances and duels won - as well as having completed more forward passes and more line-breaking passes than any other outfielder in the Premier League

Van Hecke's uncle Jan Poortvliet (centre, facing camera) was a defender in the Netherlands team which lost to Argentina in the 1978 World Cup final

Van Hecke's uncle Jan Poortvliet was a defender in the Netherlands team which made it to the World Cup final in 1978, and 30 years later had a brief spell as Southampton manager in the Championship. Jan Paul needs one more cap to match Poortvliet's tally of 19 for his country.

Blackburn boss Tony Mowbray, a fearless centre-half as a player, compared Van Hecke to another blond England legend after luring him to Ewood Park on loan from Brighton in 2021. The Seagulls had signed Van Hecke for £1.8million the year before and sold him to Spurs this summer for £54m.

'I've got to be careful I don't overbuild him as he's not our player,' said Mowbray at the time. 'But he looks like Bobby Moore out there sometimes. It's amazing to watch how composed, how calm he can be, yet he has the fire of a warrior in his belly.'

Van Hecke's vision and passing range combined with his natural aggression and appetite for sporting conflict appeals to the modern coach.

He meets the physical demands of the Premier League with relish, hailing from Arnemuiden, an isolated town of 5,000 in the province of Zeeland with a deep-rooted fishing history and a reputation for resilience through times of hardship.

It is now home to an army of devoted Van Hecke fans who cross the North Sea to watch him play at every opportunity. One hundred made the journey to see him score against Crystal Palace last Saturday.

Another element of Van Hecke's early impact in N17 has been his readiness to accept the ball, often in difficult areas, and search for forward passes through the lines.

It has led to mistakes which irritated some Spurs fans during their terrible start to the campaign, but De Zerbi demands this high-risk style and Van Hecke to his credit resisted the temptation to play with greater caution even though it would have spared him some of the criticism.

Van Hecke made such an impression on Tony Mowbray on loan at Blackburn in 2021-22 that he compared him to Bobby Moore

His impact is clear from his data. Van Hecke has played every minute of the Premier League campaign, starting the game at Manchester United last month despite returning from international duty with stitches in a wound on the top of his foot.

He has completed more forward passes (258) and more line-breaking passes (150) than any outfielder in the Premier League. Only Arsenal duo Martin Odegaard (197) and Declan Rice (177) have made more successful passes into the final third than his 174, only Manchester City's Ruben Dias (819) has played more passes than his 809, and Van Hecke leads the Spurs ranks for clearances and duels won. For good measure, he is also the club's top scorer – albeit with only two goals.

His desire to shoulder responsibility even in difficult times is exactly the type of leadership by example Spurs have lacked in recent years.

'He excelled in one-on-one defending but above all in his mentality,' Maas tells Daily Mail Sport as he reflects on Van Hecke's early development after joining NAC from amateur team VV Goes at the age of 18.

'What struck me was that when faced with setbacks, or a kick or a blow to the head on the pitch, he always got back up with even greater determination. It was as if the adrenaline helped him become unbeatable.

'That's where he channelled his energy. First at NAC in the second tier, then at Heerenveen in the Eredivisie. At Brighton, too. Step by step, he gets 10 per cent better every time because he adapts easily to his surroundings.'

There were times when the teenage Van Hecke might display frustration to be on the fringes of the team at NAC. Competition for places at the back included Colin Rosler, a graduate of the Manchester City academy where his father Uwe was a hero and who now plays in Denmark for AGF.

'Until the winter of 2019, JP was mainly a substitute and clearly struggling with that,' recalls Maas, who left the head scout's role at NAC for the same post at Heerenveen in 2021 before returning as NAC technical director two years later.

Van Hecke is Spurs' top scorer in the Premier League this season - albeit with only two goals

'It was impossible to predict he would make the upper echelons of the Premier League and the Dutch national team,' says Maas. 'But you could certainly see he had great potential'

'He felt it was unfair that he wasn't playing and went through a rough patch and was showing it. He actually lost the will to play, and I held a mirror to him once during a chat in the players' lounge and told him he had to prove himself.'

Helped by a change of head coach, Van Hecke broke into the first team and became integral to second-tier NAC's run to the semi-finals of the Dutch Cup, beating PSV Eindhoven and AZ Alkmaar before losing to Feyenoord.

His success came to personify the fighting spirit of NAC and he became the poster boy for their prolific youth development programme, with Bart Verbruggen, Van Hecke's team-mate at Brighton, also a graduate.

'It was impossible to predict he would make the upper echelons of the Premier League and the Dutch national team,' says Maas. 'But you could certainly see he had great potential and he will continue to improve because his immense drive will take him further.'

#1122. Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's  unfair trade practices.

In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.

Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."

China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."

Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.

Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:

"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.

According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.

The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.

Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.

Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.

This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.

"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Just another day in space. NASA’s Astrobee, a cubic robot around 30 centimetres across, is designed to work in the microgravity environment inside the International Space Station (ISS). Each of NASA’s three Astrobees — working autonomously, or controlled by ISS astronauts or Earth-bound flight controllers and researchers —  float around taking on tasks such as drawing up inventories and recording experiments. The robots also function as experimental subjects to test microgravity software and hardware.

The Canadian-built arm of the ISS, Canadarm2, holds a Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft during undocking operations. It was released about 420 kilometres above the North Atlantic Ocean on 9 October.

Sting mechanics. A bee’s stinger was observed in action as it injected its venom, called apitoxin, into a gel that mimics skin1. Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel, a sensory ecologist at the University of New South Wales in Canberra, and her collaborators detached the stinger from a honey bee (Apis mellifera) and studied the mechanics of its pumping mechanism. They discovered that it involves two collapsible cylinders that act as pistons.

Mourning ritual. In northwestern Namibia, Italian photographer Federico Veronesi followed tracks on a dry river bed to catch a rare glimpse of an elephant carrying a dead calf. His shot was the overall winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition, which is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. Researchers have documented a range of mourning behaviours in African elephants (Loxodonta spp.), including carrying and guarding the dead.

Francisco Negroni/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

A dung beetle (unidentified species) in Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park shot by Oscar Whitfield, who won the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.

Photo naturalist Tony Wu spent three years tracking the behaviour of eels off Japan’s southern island of Kyushu. Eventually he captured two specimens of Abbott’s moray eel (Gymnothorax eurostus) in what could be the first photo documenting their spawning behaviour. He used a red light, because the animals spawn at night and are sensitive to other colours of light. On his blog, he wrote that this was “the most difficult and challenging photographic endeavor that I have ever undertaken”.

Nature photographer Agorastos Papatsanis shone ultraviolet light on the forest floor at the foot of Mount Olympus in Greece to reveal the glowing stems of beautiful bonnet mushrooms (Mycena renati). Many fungi fluoresce under UV light — an effect that mycologists can use to help identify species.

Chilean photographer Francisco Negroni took this image of a dead puma (Puma concolor) displayed as a hunting trophy on a fence in the Patagonia region of Argentina.

The Wildlife Photographer of the Year exhibition is on until 11 July 2027 at London’s Natural History Museum.

Beautiful tech. This unusual view, of droplets of ink being squeezed through nozzles and onto paper during the printing process, won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World competition. Ole Bielfeldt, an experimental photographer in Cologne, Germany, was partially motivated by his desire to understand how inkjet printers work.

This mesmerizing web is a cross-section of a mouse eye, showing retinal blood vessels and the optic nerve.

A tardigrade moulting and laying an egg in the old skin.

Skin cells from embryonic Xenopus frogs, show cilia (green), centrioles (a type of organelle, red) and cell membranes (white).

The nuclei in this 20-day-old sea urchin larva fluoresce blue to create a doodle-like outline.

A seal louse (Antarctophthirus sp.) attached to a hair from one of the aquatic mammals.

First responders. Rescuers carry an adult female orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) across a palm-oil plantation in Laman Satong, Indonesian Borneo, on 30 September. Indonesia has been experiencing its worst wildfire season in a decade, blanketing southeast Asia in thick smoke.

Neanderthal hand. A dig in a cave in northern Spain has yielded the remains of a 46,000-year-old Neanderthal, including a well-preserved hand. The findings, which were presented in Tarragona, Spain, on 19 October and have not yet been peer reviewed, included analyses of what researchers described as well-preserved ancient DNA.

Space jellyfish. The 13 October launch of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida produced this mesmerizing show as the exhaust glistened in predawn sunlight, and was caught by NASA photographer Bill White. The rocket was headed to the ISS on a resupply mission.

Storm vision. As Typhoon Surigae lingered off the coast of Japan on 28 September, the European Space Agency’s Copernicus Sentinel-1 pictured the sea underneath it using polarized radar. The orange in this false-colour image reveals rough surface conditions caused by strong winds; the calmer seas at the eye of the storm are dark blue.

Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA

Underwater treasure trove. A stunning 57 new marine species and 5 genera spanning corals, sea cucumbers and crustaceans were identified in just two weeks at an international ‘species discovery’ workshop in Buenos Aires in July. Scientists from across Latin America and Europe gathered to study marine samples, many of which were collected by the deep-sea remotely operated vehicle SuBastian in an expedition led by the Schmidt Ocean Institute to Argentina’s Mar del Plata Canyon in August 2025. The new species include ‘Loki’, a pale sea cucumber with a blob-like body that features two stubby appendages (Peniagone sp.).

#1119. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

By the end, with Estevao – making the most of a first league start of the season – running riot and Chelsea smelling blood, Carrick would have been relieved the scoreline was not worse. Michael Carrick said he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

It left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

The Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

“Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Sometimes you get setbacks in games and you’ve got to deal with that better. I’ve not seen it [the Martinez incident] back so I don’t know if it was [a red card] or not. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

#1116. The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech

Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.

"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.

This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.

In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.

These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.

"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.

Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.

But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.

Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.

That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.

"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."

A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges" such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

#1114. Pressure mounts on under-fire Regis Le Bris as Sunderland lose again, Bournemouth's super-subs preserve their flawless start, Pierre Sage is handed a Crystal Palace lifeline after late equaliser, while Brighton win

By MILES STARFORTH and LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and WILL PICKWORTH, SPORTS REPORTER and JAMES SHARPE

Published: 15:39 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:40 EDT, 5 November 2026

Sunderland's unbeaten start to their first European campaign in 53 years was brought to an abrupt end by Dinamo Zagreb to pile more pressure on Regis Le Bris ahead of Chelsea's visit to Wearside.

The Croatian side won 2-0 to heap more misery on Le Bris and his team at the Stadium of Light following a dismal start to the season in which his team has won just one Premier League fixture.

There were Bonfire Night fireworks across Wearside, and before the game at the Stadium of Light, but not enough on the pitch from Sunderland, who only came to life after the break.

Europa League football has been an antidote to domestic doom and gloom for Sunderland fans, with the club having made a bright start to its first European campaign in 53 years by winning two and drawing one of their first three group phase fixtures.

But it was Dinamo who would light up the first half with two moments of quality from Luke Stojkovic and Dion Beljo.

Le Bris had labelled the season as 'probably the most demanding challenge Sunderland has faced in its history' before the game, which followed a 3-1 defeat by newly-promoted Coventry City. The 3-1 loss left the Carabao Cup quarter-finalists rooted to the bottom of the Premier League with just five points from nine games, and Le Bris under scrutiny ahead of a challenging run of fixtures.

Roger Le Bris is under increasing pressure at Sunderland after seeing his side lose once again

Granit Xhaka cuts a forlorn figure as Sunderland's unbeaten Europa League start ends

Le Bris, mindful of Sunday's Premier League game against fourth-placed Chelsea, made six changes against the Croatian champions, leaving top scorer Brian Brobbey on the bench along with influential midfielder Enzo Le Fee.

Le Bris also labelled the club's domestic struggles this term as 'growing pains', and Sunderland are not the first promoted club to suffer second-season syndrome. The problem for them is that they also have to contend with a lot more games due to their success last season.

The Black Cats found Dinamo, who parted company with domestic double-winning manager Mario Kovacevic following a shock defeat by newly-promoted Rudes on Saturday, hard to break down in the first 15 minutes, and when Chris Rigg did get in behind after being found by captain Granit Xhaka, Jules Ahoka could not get enough power on his header.

Dinamo's Stojkovic, however, could not have hit his effort at the other end of the pitch any better. With Wilson Isidor waiting to come back on the pitch following treatment, the visitors, backed by 1,500 noisy fans, won a corner. Xhaka headed it away from goal, but only as far as Stojkovic, who chested the ball down and superbly volleyed it past Robin Roefs to put Dinamo ahead.

Thomas Meunier then clipped the woodwork with a cross aimed for the head of Isidor before things got even worse for the home side. Kevin Danso's weak clearance found Stojkovic, who clipped the ball to Beljo, who then dinked it over Roefs to put his team in control at the break.

Le Fee was one of four players sent on by Le Bris for the second half, and a goal from Isidor - he headed Xhaka's free-kick home - was ruled out for offside a minute after the restart.

Sunderland, at least, were playing with some much-needed urgency following a lacklustre first 45 minutes, and Danso hit the crossbar during a spell of pressure from Le Bris's side.

Sunderland fans vented their frustration, both at their team and referee Andrea Colombo, as the second half wore on.

Luka Stojkovic scored Dinamo Zagreb's opener in their 2-0 win with this sublime strike

But Sunderland, for all their second-half possession, rarely tested goalkeeper Dominik Kotarski, Dinamo saw the game out to condemn Sunderland to only their second defeat in European competition, the last having come against Sporting Lisbon in the 1973-74 season.

Le Bris must now quickly pick up his side ahead of the visit of Chelsea.

Progression in Europe is important for the club, and Sunderland should still avoid elimination when the Europa League's group phase ends, but nowhere near as important as preserving its Premier League status.

Forget the icing on the cake, the Cherries joint-top, second on goal difference, of the Europa League after their come-from-behind 3-1 win at Sparta Prague.

After winning just one of their opening eight matches in all competitions, Bournemouth have now won seven on the bounce thanks to second-half goals from Tyler Adams, Evanilson and Rayan. All three came on as second-half substitutes to underline the quality that Marco Rose has at his disposal.

'You can't get too comfortable. You have to continue to hold that standard,' reflected Adams post-match. 'That winning mentality becomes continuous, especially when you're playing every three days.'

Rose, who made eight changes to his XI, will be delighted with his side's fight but will also thank Sparta centre-back Tobias Guddal who inexplicably got himself sent off in the first half for two avoidable yellow cards.

Prior to Guddal's red card, Sparta were in the ascendancy and should have taken the lead when striker Jonatan Braut Brunes, Erling Haaland's cousin, inexplicably put wide a tap-in in the opening two minutes.

That was the biggest chance in the match until Bournemouth were awarded a penalty midway through the first half. Former Liverpool defender Ki-Jana Hoever, who is on loan from Wolves, was booked for a handball in the box. Lewis Cook's stutter run-up fooled Jakub Surovcik but saw his low effort hit the inside of the left-hand post before rolling out of play.

Evanilson was on the scoresheet as Bournemouth came from behind to win at Sparta Prague

Fellow substitute Tyler Adams (second left) started the visitors' 3-1 comeback with this finish

Rayan celebrates after adding a third for Bournemouth to complete their memorable victory

If Cook was unlucky, there was no element of luck to Sparta breaking the deadlock. Counter-attacking from a Cherries' corner, Surovcik threw the ball out to Ebrima Singhateh inside his own half. The impressive winger shrugged off Cook before beginning his brilliant run, which included slaloming in between Bournemouth players, and scoring. It was a goal befitting of the Champions League, let alone the Europa League.

Sparta's joy was short-lived as Guddal, who had already been booked for a foul on Ben Gannon-Doak, then inexplicably brought down Alvaro Rodriguez.

Rose turned to his bench at half-time and all of his changes worked as they pressed Sparta into mistakes. Adams was the beneficiary for their first goal as he scored with a low right-footed shot from outside the box 12 minutes after coming on.

With 10 minutes remaining Evanilson put the visitors ahead with a sublime curled effort into the far corner with no backlift.

'He's on fire right now, but you see him do it every day in training,' Adams purred about his team-mate. For him to do it in a game is no surprise. He has so much quality.

'Whenever he gets in and around the box, we're confident he's going to find the back of the net.'

Ebrima Singhateh scored the goal of the game to give Sparta the lead after a stunning solo run

Before Singhateh's stunner, Lewis Cook saw his penalty hit the inside of the post and go out

Evanilson then turned provider, via a neat one-two, to see Rayan score from distance.

The result means it's four out of four in the Europa League for the European debutants. With Celta Vigo away next after the international break, don't be surprised if it's five out of five.

As the fourth official signalled three minutes of added time, Pierre Sage may have been cursing his luck on the Selhurst Park touchline.

Although he has been hampered by the absences of Jean-Philippe Mateta, Ismaila Sarr and Dean Henderson at points this season, plus a transfer strategy that has left him shorn of experience and quality in key areas, the Frenchman was approaching a record of eight defeats in 13 league and European games.

Two seasons ago, Crystal Palace's hierarchy kept faith with Oliver Glasner when his side won one of their first 13 matches - a record that preceded the greatest 18 months in the club's history - but Sage was running out of time to prove he deserved a similar demonstration of trust.

Enter Daichi Kamada, Palace's best player here, as he finished calmly through the legs of Hoffenheim goalkeeper Oliver Baumann to rescue a valuable point for his side.

But this was a let-off for Sage on a night that had felt like it could precede the final days of his tenure, and he must now summon an improved display against Liverpool this weekend.

'Conceding early in the game was difficult because we had to push to come back,' Sage said post-match. 'But we scored at the end, and the players deserved it because they didn't give up.'

Daichi Kamara earned Crystal Palace a point in second-half stoppage-time against Hoffenheim

Hoffenheim took the lead in the 1-1 encounter when Alexander Prass (second right) scored

Palace's equaliser came when down to 10 men after Adam Wharton's (centre) earlier dismissal

There was nothing to sum up Palace's predicament quite like Alexander Prass' early opener. Having started well - with Kamada having a goal ruled out for offside - Quinten Timber saw a penalty appeal waved away before the out-of-form Adam Wharton was dispossessed. The German side broke forward at electric speed and Prass' effort squirmed through Henderson.

It was an all too familiar story as Palace's defence - weakened by Sage's decision to leave Axel Disasi out of his squad in what he later labelled 'an internal decision' - again looked ill-equipped for the challenge in hand.

'Offensively we did better than our two previous games, but we have to continue to improve defensively because we gave too much space to them,' Sage added.

'When we defend too much, we have no chance to exist in the game, and when we try to attack a little bit, we are quickly open. You don't exist in the game when you don't attack. For this team the best way to defend is to keep the ball with efficiency.'

The hosts were careless on the ball though, doing little to improve the subdued atmosphere at Selhurst Park, and although Yeremy Pino and Kamada spurned good chances, Hoffenheim appeared to have closed out the game.

Palace's late equaliser eases the pressure on under-fire boss Pierre Sage for now

Palace's frustration was demonstrated by four yellow cards in seven minutes, before Wharton received a second shortly after to compound their misery.

The home faithful threatened to turn restless and it looked like the night would end in disappointment, until Kamada's strike gave Sage a lifeline.

Trust Pascal Gross to seize the moment. For a little over an hour, Brighton toiled and laboured in pursuit of the goal that would ignite their European dreams.

The Seagulls have made light work of the Premier League, these vanquishers of Arsenal and Manchester City and now are starting to stretch their dominance across the continent.

Gnarly minnows Getafe love to make life deeply unpleasant for their opponents and Brighton, for all their energy and endeavour, looked destined to be unable to find the answers.

Yet there he was, this 35-year-old starting a remarkable 16th straight game of the season when it mattered. There was Gross, afforded too much space on the left, allowed to spot the run of Joao Costinha towards the back post.

Naturally, the German landed his raking cross right on Costinha's head. The wing-back nodded it across goal for Malick Yalcouye to send a header of his own into the top corner to win it and send Brighton, who are yet to concede in the competition, into the Conference League play-off places and their fans dreaming of European glory.

'The fans should dream and, hopefully at one point, maybe we fulfil their dream,' said Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler.

Malick Yalcouye (centre) scored the winner as Brighton won 1-0 at Getafe in the Europa Conference League

'We focus on work and we focus on the things we can control. We didn't play our best game. We had a few moments where we were lazy with the easy things. We didn't do the simple things on the highest level. But we kept a clean sheet, scored in the right moment and I think we deserve to win this game.'

Getafe, this modest club from the outskirts of Madrid, have long lived in the shadow of their monumental neighbours Real and Atletico but have also earned a famous reputation for a good old-fashioned giant killing.

They once beat Barcelona 4-0 here to overturn a three-goal deficit to reach the Copa del Rey final and then did them again in the league the following season. They went up the road to the Bernabeu in March and came away with three points.

Brighton, meanwhile, have made such a habit of turning over the bigger boys that, for the Seagulls, it's stopped becoming that extraordinary.

They mix so frequently among the giants these days that it's often easy to see the Seagulls as ones themselves. Getafe certainly would.

What was always going to be fascinating was the clash of styles. Brighton, with their relentless press and free-flowing football under Fabian Hurzeler, against a physical Getafe side that boasts the lowest possession and pass success rate in La Liga. There's a reason their players have already been shown six red cards

This Brighton and Hove Albion title challenge – as it must now be classed – flies in the face of the saying that money always talks in football. Ayari cost £3.5m from Swedish club AIK and scored in the 5-0 wins over Coventry and Palace, and now has this winner to add to his collection. It could keep them at the top end of the table for a good while longer. In Fabian Hürzeler they have one of the brightest young coaches in the Premier League and he has a squad that are all on the same page.

Leicester upset the odds 10 years ago with a settled team, while this Brighton team has a deeper squad. When the substitutes came on in the second half, they slotted into a well-rehearsed system.

“We faced adversity. There was a little bit of luck but in the end they deserved it because they worked hard for it,” said Hürzeler. “I want players who want to compete, to dominate. #1110. FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football

Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for better structures globally.

At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first in South America, will be the last with 32 teams and is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is historic, as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.

But even for the handful of players who make it out of these youth tournaments to a professional career, creating a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.

The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The global average salary is $2,600 (€2,300) a month, but the range varies drastically across the world. In Eastern Europe, for example, that average is $880 per month. In Africa, it is $432, but in North America it is just under $6,000.

"I think what you also find in the women's game is the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW.

"In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and not being paid at all."

With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement.

"Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures — including extra workload and social media abuse — but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier — in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year — the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German football association rule shows that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

"The facilities and the staff members," Nicole Anyomi told DW, were a factor in her making a recent move to London City Lionesses. "We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Ultimately, the faster the game grows, the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

#1105. Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The abandonment of villages in Japan is changing ecosystems. Studies are finding that biodiversity has declined in places that people have left behind.Credit: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Bloomberg/Getty

The idea that humanity is separate from the rest of the planet is deep-rooted, but wrong. Indeed, for most of human history, this has not been the case1. Many landscapes seen by European colonists as ‘wilderness’ were in fact tended by Indigenous people. This includes North America’s wildflower-studded oak savannahs and Australia’s fire-maintained ecosystems. Worldwide, traditional agricultural practices — which have been used for millennia, in some cases2 — have created ecological niches that support insects, amphibians, birds and plants, many of which have evolved together with humans.

When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

People have always cleared land to some extent. But the scale of this practice has been unprecedented since the beginning of industrialization in the mid-eighteenth century, and especially since the onset of industrial farming. Intensive land conversion is the biggest driver of biodiversity loss. It’s a key reason why countries agreed four years ago to protect 30% of land and water habitats by 2030 (also called the 30 × 30 target).

That goal, however, explicitly did not intend for protected areas to be human-free zones3. Now, as Nature reports in a News feature, evidence is emerging that biodiversity does not necessarily thrive in places that humans leave behind. In Japan, where entire villages are being abandoned because of rural depopulation, the decline in traditional rice-farming practices and woodland management is reducing habitat availability for many birds, insects and plants that thrive in flooded paddies, along field margins or in open-canopy forests.

This example and others show that protected areas need humans to be responsible for specific tasks. These jobs include water management, the provision of grazing animals and ecologically informed forestry, such as using prescribed burning to prevent catastrophic megafires similar to those the world is seeing increasingly. The Americas, Europe and Australia will need many thousands of fire-trained professionals in the coming decades.

Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Land-tending practices also include traditional foraging and planting, the building of clam gardens on the coast and cutting down trees and shrubs to thin woodlands and stimulate fresh growth. Such work must be informed by modern ecology and conservation biology — which increasingly incorporate lessons from ecological knowledge that comes from, in some cases, millennia of practical field experiments.

These practices also need to be funded. Traditional farming and land-management techniques are expensive compared with industrial agriculture, which requires less labour and has huge yields. If humanity wants to preserve these traditional relationships with the planet and the biodiversity they support, governments will have to subsidize this work directly.

This is already being done in a limited way, through grants to farmers and in agricultural-biodiversity schemes. However, nations should consider providing robust and comprehensive support. Programmes could be based on the US Civilian Conservation Corps — created during the Great Depression in the 1930s — although standards would need to be updated to improve diversity and equity, and activities would have to be supported by evidence.

Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix it

Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix it

At a time of mass unemployment in the private sector, the corps was a publicly funded job-creation scheme that employed three million young men. Working in teams, they planted trees, prepared terraced fields, built roads and trails, erected fire towers and otherwise tended to US natural resources between 1933 and 1942.

Today, artificial intelligence is raising concerns not only about its environmental impacts4, but also that it could cause another phase of high levels of unemployment. Governments looking to establish schemes that could buffer their workforces against job losses associated with technological changes should consider investing in people’s relationships with land, water and biodiversity. It would be a mutually beneficial outcome: for people and the ecosystems we inhabit.

#1099. Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief

As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

A special player because of the character and he has unique characteristics.

“For James Maddison or the players who are coming from a long injury, they have to work more than the other players, but he has already four or five weeks he is working very hard and consistently.”

While Tottenham are chasing a third successive league victory for the first time in 616 day, De Zerbi insisted there will be no complacency. “For me nothing has changed. We started this pre-season with a long project and we have to stay calm and clear in the head to work to build something better than when we came here,” he said. “One win or one defeat more, nothing will change. We have to analyse to improve the results but to improve the results we have to improve all aspects.”

Pierre Sage, the Palace manager, lightened the load after knocking Fulham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek but seemed surprised that the fans have remained so supportive. “It’s always a good sign,” he said. “I appreciate it [singing his name at Craven Cottage] very much and I can thank them but I prefer they are with the team than me alone. Because I’m the manager, but I’m not the most important part of the team, of the performance and the result. I think the players need it more than me but it’s really appreciated from me.”

Asked what he has learnt about fan sentiment from looking at social media, he said: “I think they understood what happened, why we are not perfect at the moment. We don’t care who is the most responsible for the situation. I take the responsibility. I have no problem with that. I just want people to understand what we do and why.”

Two changes from the starting line-up that took on Newcastle: captain Dean Henderson is back in goal and Oscar Mingueza replaces Anan Khalaili at right wing-back.

#1093. 'Why are you speaking? F*** off!': Kevin De Bruyne at centre of Napoli dressing room meltdown as 'divided' squad lurches towards 'disaster'... with an 'every man for himself' culture setting in at Italian giants

Published: 03:23 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 05:08 EDT, 6 November 2026

Kevin De Bruyne was told to 'f*** off' repeatedly during Napoli's 4-1 thrashing against Porto on Wednesday, with a dressing room crisis heating up at the club.

The Napoli squad has become increasingly fractured in recent weeks, according to the Italian media, with an 'every man for himself' culture developing into a 'disaster'.

Napoli sit eighth in Serie A under new manager Massimiliano Allegri – just two seasons after winning the title under Antonio Conte – and are near the bottom of the Champions League table after three defeats in four games.

Their cracks are showing on the pitch, with striker Lorenzo Lucca yelling at De Bruyne: 'Why are you speaking? F*** off!' during their Porto drubbing.

The pair squared up to each other and Lucca shouted his expletive command three times before they went their separate ways.

After the match, Matteo Politano told Sky Sport Italia: 'It would be nice if a few other teammates came here to give an explanation and not just us Italians, but never mind, I never hide my face.'

Kevin De Bruyne was told to 'f*** off' three times by team-mate Lorenzo Lucca during Napoli's 4-1 defeat by Porto on Wednesday

There is said to be a rift developing between Napoli's native stars and foreign players

La Gazzetta dello Sport reported that Politano was calling out Cameroonian star Frank Anguissa and Kosovan Amir Rrahmani, both two-time title winners with the club.

Politano added: 'The attitude is one that a team like ours cannot have at this level. I was not attacking anyone, we have a squad that is struggling, but we need to come together and think about this next game before the break for international duty.

'Hopefully we can recover a few players during that spell and then our season can really begin.'

There is a 'divide' between the Italian group of players and foreigners, La Gazzetta dello Sport reports, though it is mostly down to frustration with results.

Individuals such as De Bruyne, Rasmus Hojlund, and Stanislav Lobotka are more 'reserved personalities' who have reportedly not bonded as well with their team-mates away from the field.

Scott McTominay, who has an ally in fellow Scottish player Billy Gilmour, said after the Porto loss: 'Of course I’m angry.

'We lost 4-1 in the Champions League; there’s nothing to smile about. For us, it’s go on and try to figure out how to fix it.

'We’ve had a lot of injuries, a lot of important players you can’t change; attacking players as well. Let’s not beat around the bush; we’ve got a lot of injuries, and that makes a big difference whenever you come into play every three days.

Napoli have had a rough start to the season under new manager Massimiliano Allegri - despite him being a legendary coach in Italy

'So, things like these can make a huge difference for the team when the same players are playing over and over again. People need to understand that, but we also need to do better. First and foremost, we need to do better, injuries in football are part of it, but we have too many.'

Their dressing room troubles have dragged on for a while. Last season, Conte complained of a lack of unity after they signed nine players on the back of their Scudetto. They still managed to finish second, but it was a turbulent ride.

'Nine new players were too many. We weren't balanced,' he said at the time.

'I experience the dressing room every day, so I say certain things; we mustn't despair. We'll try to recreate last year's chemistry.'

In one match against AC Milan, De Bruyne threw a tantrum after being subbed off by Conte.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.
